newsitem.title: USA: Albright takes hard line in NATO-Russia row.
newsitem.headline: Albright takes hard line in NATO-Russia row.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday launched a campaign for Senate support on enlarging NATO, ruling out compromise on key Russian demands over its ties with an expanded alliance.
Albright said she would go to Moscow next week to address outstanding differences, which include Russian demands for restrictions on the build-up of forces in new NATO members.

"Russia would ... like us to make absolute commitments in the (proposed Russia-NATO) charter about the deployment of nuclear and conventional forces on the territory's new members," she told the Senate Armed Services Committee.
"But we will not compromise on this issue," she said.
Albright said NATO would like to have an agreement to sign in Paris on May 27 formalising future relations between Moscow and the alliance, as Russia has suggested.
President Boris Yeltsin and other Russian officials raised expectations such a charter would be completed by that date saying last week they would be ready to sign it then.
But U.S. officials said the date is uncertain and Russia's demand for binding guarantees remains a stumbling block.
The decision on new members, most likely Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, will be made formally at a summit of NATO's 16 leaders in Madrid in July.
Moscow is asking for commitments that the new members, will not be allowed to upgrade their military facilities in any way to bring them in line with other NATO countries.
In addition, Russia wants an explicit commitment from the alliance to say it will "never" station nuclear weapons on the territory of new member countries.

Albright told the Senate: "All we have done and all we will do is to restate unilaterally existing NATO policy: that in the current and foreseeable security environment, we have no plan, no need and no intention to station nuclear weapons in the new member countries, nor do we contemplate permanently stationing substantial combat forces." Albright said.

"The only binding limits on conventional forces in Europe will be set as we adapt the CFE (Conventional Forces in Europe) treaty, with central European countries and all the other signatories at the table," she said.

President Bill Clinton has taken the lead in pressing the alliance to take in its first new members since the Cold War ended and considers enlargement one of most significant foreign and defence policy issues of this era.

Russia, a vestige of the former Soviet superpower, strongly opposes NATO expansion into its onetime Warsaw Pact allies but has come to accept that as inevitable and is pushing for the best deal it can get.
Defence Secretary William Cohen, who testified along with Albright, underscored that "NATO will not accept any limits on its infrastructure."
Albright said Clinton has been absolutely clear with Yeltsin "about the lines we will not cross" as a new Russia-NATO partnership is established.

This includes assertions that enlargment will go forward regardless of whether a charter is agreed upon, that no European nation will be excluded from potential NATO membership, that new members will have full alliance rights and benefits and that Russia will not have a veto in NATO affairs.

While NATO wants Russia to be a full participant in European security, debate over the alliance should not be reduced to a debate about Russia, Albright said. She said Russian democracy is not at stake in the enlargement decision.
Increasingly Washington intellectuals and columnists have raised doubts about the wisdom of NATO enlargement, and Albright acknowledged these sceptics.

But she argued that if it did not expand, "NATO would be stuck in the past, risking irrelevance, even dissolution. Our leadership in Europe will be compromised and relations with our traditional allies would deteriorate."
"Confidence would crumble in central Europe, leading to a search for security by other means, including arms build-ups and increased tensions between neighbours," she said.
Not to expand would "validate the dividing line (across Europe) Stalin imposed in 1945," she said.
